body:
The reinterpretation of religious traditions

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, Indian thinkers reassessed religious practices in response to social inequality, colonial rule, modern education and the growth of printing.

Reformers adopted different approaches. Some sought to reinterpret ancient scriptures, others advocated a return to what they considered original religious teachings, and others challenged traditional structures of caste and gender inequality.

Brahmo Samaj

Raja Rammohun Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha at Calcutta in 1828. It subsequently became known as the Brahmo Samaj.

He emphasised belief in one God, rational religious inquiry and opposition to practices that he regarded as unjust or unsupported by authentic religious teachings.

His campaign against sati included arguments based on ancient religious texts and the moral rights of women. The practice was prohibited in the Bengal Presidency in 1829 under Governor-General William Bentinck.

The Brahmo movement also supported women's education and wider social reform. Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen became important later leaders.

Prarthana Samaj

The Prarthana Samaj was established in Bombay in 1867 by Atmaram Pandurang. Mahadev Govind Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar were among its influential members.

It advocated devotion to one God and worked against social practices such as caste restrictions, child marriage and prohibitions on widow remarriage. It supported education and reform while drawing upon existing Indian devotional traditions.

Arya Samaj and its Gujarat connection

Swami Dayanand Saraswati was born as Mool Shankar at Tankara in present-day Morbi district, Gujarat, in 1824.

He founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875. He regarded the Vedas as authoritative and advocated a return to Vedic teachings. He rejected image worship and criticised hereditary caste distinctions, superstition and harmful social customs.

His important work Satyarth Prakash presents his religious and reformist ideas.

The Arya Samaj supported education, social reform and the reinterpretation of religious practice. Its activities influenced modern educational institutions and nationalist thought.

The Brahmo Samaj emphasised monotheism and rational religious reform. The Arya Samaj emphasised the authority of the Vedas. Both advocated reform, but they did not follow identical philosophical approaches.

Ramakrishna and Swami Vivekananda

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa was a 19th-century Bengali religious teacher whose spiritual outlook emphasised religious experience, devotion and recognition of different paths towards the divine.

His disciple Swami Vivekananda presented Vedantic ideas to wider Indian and international audiences. His participation in the World's Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893 became an important landmark in the international presentation of Indian religious thought.

Vivekananda advocated Practical Vedanta, connecting spiritual understanding with service to humanity, education and social uplift.

He founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897. The organisation brought together spiritual discipline and humanitarian activities, including education, healthcare and relief work.

Other reformist approaches

Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 to challenge caste inequality and hereditary social privilege. His reform activities, undertaken alongside Savitribai Phule, emphasised education and social justice.

Muslim reform initiatives also took different forms. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan promoted modern education through the Aligarh movement. Other reform traditions, including the Deoband movement, emphasised religious learning and Islamic scholarship.

These movements demonstrate that religious reform was not confined to a single community or a uniform intellectual approach.

Selected reform organisations

OrganisationYearFounder or principal figureEmphasis
Brahmo Samaj1828Rammohun RoyMonotheism and religious reform
Prarthana Samaj1867Atmaram PandurangDevotion and social reform
Satyashodhak Samaj1873Jyotirao PhuleSocial equality and opposition to caste injustice
Arya Samaj1875Dayanand SaraswatiVedic authority and reform
Ramakrishna Mission1897Swami VivekanandaPractical Vedanta and service

Gandhian thought and religious ethics

Mahatma Gandhi drew upon several Indian religious and philosophical traditions. His ethical thought combined truth, non-violence, self-discipline, religious tolerance and concern for human welfare.

The Jain thinker Shrimad Rajchandra exercised an important spiritual influence on Gandhi. Their association helped deepen Gandhi's understanding of self-restraint, non-attachment and spiritual inquiry.

Gandhi also drew inspiration from the Bhagavad Gita, particularly its teaching concerning action without selfish attachment, and from the devotional and ethical heritage of Gujarat.

He transformed Ahimsa from a principle of personal ethical discipline into a central principle of political and social action.

Satyagraha is the disciplined pursuit of truth through non-violent resistance to injustice. It seeks moral transformation rather than destruction of the opponent.

For Gandhi, religious life was closely connected with the service of others. The devotional ideal expressed in Narsinh Mehta's Vaishnav Jan To became particularly compatible with his emphasis on empathy and social responsibility.

Prelims focus

  • Rammohun Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828.
  • Prarthana Samaj was established in Bombay in 1867.
  • Dayanand Saraswati was born at Tankara and founded Arya Samaj in 1875.
  • Satyarth Prakash was written by Dayanand Saraswati.
  • Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
  • Gandhi was spiritually influenced by Shrimad Rajchandra and the Bhagavad Gita.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts III, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, pp. 94–108; NCERT, Class 10, India and the Contemporary World II, Nationalism in India, section 1.1, The Idea of Satyagraha, pp. 54–55; Press Information Bureau, 12 February 2024, address on the 200th birth anniversary of Maharshi Dayanand Saraswati at Tankara; Belur Math, Swami Vivekananda, section on founding the Ramakrishna Mission; Shrimad Rajchandra Mission Dharampur, Shrimadji and Gandhiji, including extracts from Gandhi's autobiography; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Religious Reform Movements and the Development of Modern Indian Thought

body:
Why the traditions must be distinguished

Indian religious and philosophical traditions frequently use similar terms, including karma, liberation, devotion and non-violence. However, the meaning of these terms and the methods through which spiritual objectives are achieved differ across traditions.

A clear comparison therefore requires attention to the particular doctrine, text, teacher and historical tradition involved.

Vedic, Buddhist and Jain approaches

FeatureUpanishadic and Vedantic traditionsBuddhismJainism
Vedic authorityAcceptedNot acceptedNot accepted
Individual selfAtman; interpreted differently by Vedanta schoolsNo eternal, unchanging selfEnduring individual Jiva
Spiritual problemIgnorance and bondageSuffering sustained by craving and ignoranceKarmic bondage of the soul
PathKnowledge, action or devotion, depending on traditionNoble Eightfold PathRight faith, knowledge and conduct
LiberationMokshaNirvanaMoksha

Buddhism and Jainism both questioned Vedic ritual authority, recognised karma and rebirth, developed monastic communities and encouraged ethical conduct. However, Buddhism advocated the Middle Way, while Jain monastic discipline placed greater emphasis on strict austerity and minimising harm to living beings.

Different meanings of the Three Jewels

TraditionThree Jewels
BuddhismBuddha, Dhamma and Sangha
JainismRight faith, right knowledge and right conduct

The same expression, Triratna, has distinct meanings in Buddhism and Jainism. The Buddhist formulation identifies the spiritual teacher, teaching and community, whereas the Jain formulation identifies the conditions for liberation.

Important concepts that must not be confused

ConceptTradition or thinkerCentral meaning
Purusha and PrakritiSamkhyaConsciousness and nature
AnattaBuddhismAbsence of a permanent self
AnekantavadaJainismMany-sided nature of reality
SyadvadaJainismQualified statements
NiyatiAjivikaPredetermined destiny
AdvaitaShankaracharyaUltimate non-duality
PushtiVallabhacharyaDivine grace
Nishkama KarmaBhagavad GitaAction without selfish attachment to its fruits
TawhidIslamUnity of God
SatyagrahaMahatma GandhiNon-violent pursuit of truth and justice

Religious ideas and literary traditions

Religious philosophy influenced both classical and regional literature. The form of a literary work often reflects its purpose.

Vedic hymns preserved ritual and religious knowledge. Upanishadic dialogues explored philosophical questions. Buddhist Jataka stories communicated moral teachings through narrative. Jain Agamas preserved religious teachings, while illuminated Jain manuscripts combined literature and painting.

Bhakti poetry used forms such as the Pada, Abhanga, Vachana, Doha, Prabhatiya and Garbi to communicate devotion and ethical ideas. Sufi poetry and musical traditions similarly provided accessible forms of spiritual expression.

Gujarat's place in Indian intellectual and religious history

Gujarat provides important examples of the wider development of Indian religious traditions. Its heritage includes Ashokan inscriptions, Buddhist monasteries, Jain centres of pilgrimage and scholarship, Vaishnava devotional literature, Sufi shrines and Parsi religious settlements.

Tankara, MorbiBirthplace of Dayanand Saraswati
Udvada, ValsadParsi religious heritage

Continuity and change across traditions

Ancient Indian philosophy investigated reality, knowledge, moral action and liberation. Religious institutions preserved these ideas through education, worship and scholarship. Medieval devotional movements communicated spiritual ideas through regional languages, music and community life. Modern reformers reinterpreted religious traditions in relation to social equality, education and humanitarian service.

These developments did not follow a simple pattern in which one tradition completely replaced another. Older and newer traditions often continued alongside each other, interacting while retaining their distinct beliefs and institutions.

Prelims focus

  • Acceptance of Vedic authority distinguishes the classical Astika schools from Nastika traditions.
  • Buddhism rejects a permanent self; Jainism accepts enduring individual souls.
  • The Buddhist and Jain formulations of Triratna are different.
  • Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti differ in their understanding of divine attributes and form.
  • Gujarat's religious heritage includes Buddhist, Jain, Hindu, Sufi and Parsi traditions.
  • Trap: Similar religious terminology does not necessarily indicate identical philosophical doctrines.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 7 and Class 10, chapters on religious sects, saints and literary heritage; Gujarat Tourism, Buddhist Circuit and Religious Sites; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
